content: Recurrent idiopathic epistaxis in children refers to repeated episodes of nasal bleeding in individuals up to the age of 16, where no specific underlying cause has been identified. While nosebleeds are a common occurrence in children and often resolve spontaneously or with simple measures like pinching the nose, more severe and recurrent cases may necessitate medical intervention. However, there is currently no consensus on the effectiveness of the various clinical treatments available for managing this condition. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of different interventions for managing recurrent idiopathic epistaxis in children. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, and others, to identify relevant published and unpublished trials. The most recent search was completed on March 5, 2012. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with or without blinding, that assessed any surgical or medical intervention for treating recurrent idiopathic epistaxis in children. These trials were required to report or allow calculation of the frequency and severity of nasal bleeding episodes following treatment. Two authors independently reviewed the full-text articles of potentially relevant trials and applied the inclusion criteria. The trials were assessed for risk of bias using the Cochrane methodology. Data extraction was performed in a standardized manner by one author and rechecked by the other. Investigators were contacted when additional information was needed. Due to the heterogeneity of the treatments, procedures, and quality of the included trials, a meta-analysis was not performed. Instead, a narrative overview of the results was presented. Five studies, including four RCTs and one quasi-randomized controlled trial, met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 468 participants. The interventions compared in these studies included 0.5% neomycin + 0.1% chlorhexidine (Naseptin®) cream versus no treatment, Vaseline® petroleum jelly versus no treatment, 75% versus 95% silver nitrate nasal cautery, and silver nitrate cautery combined with Naseptin® versus Naseptin® alone. The quasi-randomized controlled trial compared Naseptin® antiseptic cream with silver nitrate cautery. The overall results were inconclusive, with no statistically significant differences observed between most of the compared treatments at the end of the trials. However, 75% silver nitrate was found to be more effective than 95% silver nitrate two weeks after application. Specifically, 88% of children treated with 75% silver nitrate experienced complete resolution of epistaxis, compared to 65% in the group treated with 95% silver nitrate (P = 0.01). No serious adverse effects were reported for any of the interventions. However, children who underwent silver nitrate cautery reported pain despite the use of local anesthetic. Pain scores were significantly lower in those treated with 75% silver nitrate, with a mean score of 1 compared to a mean score of 5 in the 95% silver nitrate group (P = 0.001). The risk of bias assessment revealed that two RCTs had a low risk of bias, two had an unclear risk of bias, and the quasi-randomized controlled trial had a high risk of bias. In conclusion, the optimal management of recurrent idiopathic epistaxis in children remains uncertain. However, if silver nitrate nasal cautery is performed, 75% silver nitrate is preferable to 95% due to its greater short-term effectiveness and lower associated pain. High-quality randomized controlled trials with a follow-up period of at least one year are needed to better assess the relative benefits of the various treatments currently in use.
